t: Sum Of Special Evenly-Spaced Elements In Array — Square Root Decomposition on Strides
o: Each query [x, y] asks for nums[x] + nums[x+y] + nums[x+2y] + ... up to the end of the array, modulo $10^9+7$. Example 1 (nums = [0..7]): query [0,3] collects indices 0, 3, 6 → 9; [5,1] sweeps 5, 6, 7 → 18; [4,2] hits 4 and 6 → 10. Example 2's single query [0,7] picks indices 0 and 7 → 100 + 203 = 303. Naively a query reads about n/y entries, which is fatal when many of the 150000 queries use tiny strides (a stride-1 query alone touches all 50000 entries). The classic fix balances the two extremes: precompute, for every stride y ≤ √n, a suffix table dp[y][j] = nums[j] + dp[y][j+y] so those queries become O(1); strides y > √n are simulated directly, costing fewer than √n reads each. Preprocessing costs O(n·√n) ≈ 10^7 work for n = 50000 — comfortably fast, with memory as the main budget to watch.
k: A query with large stride y touches at most n/y indices, so big strides are cheap to simulate directly.
For every small stride y ≤ B ≈ √n, precompute dp[y][j] = (nums[j] + dp[y][j+y]) mod p once; those queries then answer in O(1).
Balancing gives O(n·B) preprocessing and O(q·(n/B)) querying; B = √n minimizes the sum.

a.i: Walk the indices x, x+y, x+2y, ... accumulating values until leaving the array. This is the literal reading of the statement and correct in all cases, but adversarial inputs (many stride-1 queries over a long array) drive it to billions of additions.
s: For each query (x, y), initialize an accumulator s = 0.
Step j from x by y while j < n, adding nums[j] to s.
Append s mod 1e9+7 to the answers.
a.t: O(q · n) worst case — a stride-1 query reads the entire array

a.n: Approach 2: Precompute Small Strides, Simulate Large Ones
a.i: Choose threshold B ≈ ⌈√n⌉. For each stride y ≤ B fill a right-to-left suffix table so dp[y][j] holds the sum of nums[j], nums[j+y], ... modulo p — O(B·n) time and memory. Queries with y ≤ B read one cell; queries with y > B hop directly, visiting fewer than n/y < B positions. Both branches are then bounded by roughly √n work per query, and total cost stays around 10^7 operations.
s: For every y in 1..B, sweep j from n−1 down to 0 setting dp[y][j] = (nums[j] + (j + y < n ? dp[y][j+y] : 0)) mod 1e9+7.
Answer query (x, y) with y ≤ B as dp[y][x].
Answer query (x, y) with y > B by hopping j = x, x+y, ... and reducing the accumulated sum modulo 1e9+7.
a.t: O(n·B + q·B) ≈ O((n + q)·√n) — preprocessing fills B tables of length n; each large-stride query walks fewer than B entries
a.sp: O(n·B) ≈ O(n√n) — roughly 225 tables of length n (use 32-bit entries; values fit under 2^31)

w: Name the technique out loud — square-root decomposition via threshold balancing — because recognizing when O(√n)-style preprocessing beats segment trees is the real lesson here. Pitfalls: applying the modulus inconsistently between the tables and the direct loop; blowing memory by picking B too large (tables hold ~B·n integers); using 32-bit accumulation for direct sums of up to 5·10^4 values near 10^9 (needs 64-bit / safe integers before the final reduction); and swapping the query pair order ([x, y], not [y, x]). Edge cases: strides larger than n (the loop visits exactly one element), starts near the end of the array, and all-zero arrays. Follow-ups: support point updates (each update invalidates one entry per stored stride — O(√n) per update), or generalize the query to arbitrary arithmetic progressions with start and stop.
